newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Plan approved to demobilise bulk of Angolan troops.
newsitem.headline: Plan approved to demobilise bulk of Angolan troops.

text.p: A plan to demobilise thousands of Angolan government and former rebel UNITA troops within seven months has been approved by a technical group, a United Nations official said on Wednesday.
"The plan calls for the demobilisation of UNITA troops to begin by March 1," said Rosa Malango, technical adviser on demobilisation and reintegration for the U.N.'s humanitarian unit.
A joint ceasefire commission including the government, UNITA and the U.N. is expected to give the plan the final go-ahead on Thursday.
"After 50 percent of UNITA troops are demobilised we will begin with the government troops in Luanda. The whole process will be done in seven months.
"We feel confident that the plan will be approved by the joint commission on Thursday," she said.
The Angolan demobilisation programme is months behind schedule after problems were found in a timetable approved last year.

The revised plan calls for the immediate demobilisation of UNITA forces at three U.N.-sponsored assembly camps in Huambo and Kwanza Sul provinces. Troops at Vila Nova in Huambo have been disarmed at the camp since 1995.
There are a total of 15 camps throughout the country with more than 65,000 troops awaiting demobilisation.
The demobilisation is to coincide with the scheduled withdrawal of U.N. troops from Angola at the end of February.
Assembly areas in Huambo and Kwanza Sul are occupied by a battalion from Uruguay scheduled to be the first to withdraw from Angola.

The mandate of the current U.N. mission, the largest in the world at some 7,000 people, expires on February 28. Although the mandate is likely to be extended the U.N. has made it clear that the mission will be scaled down.

The two sides in Angola's civil war, which started on independence from Portugal in 1975, signed a peace accord in the Zambian capital Lusaka in 1994. Under the agreement both sides have to demobilise a total of 100,000 soldiers.
